title: Russia’s Air War Aims to Bleed Ukraine Dry
gist: Fredrik Wesslau argues that with its ground advance stalled, Russia has shifted to a systematic air war on Ukraine's economic infrastructure (fuel, rail, ports, steel, data centers, utilities), enabled by ~100 ballistic missiles a month versus US Patriot output of about half that. He calls for Patriot swaps and licensed PAC-3 production, deep strikes on Russian missile production, a CBAM waiver for Ukrainian steel, and pre-emptive EU preparation for a winter refugee exodus.

themes.theme: Russia's new theory of victory: economic strangulation

insights.claim: After Ukrainian forces stopped and partly reversed Russia's ground advance, the Kremlin shifted to a theory of victory based on widening missile and drone strikes to paralyze Ukraine's economy, society, and state functioning before winter.
insights.so_what: A strategy aimed at economic collapse rather than territory pushes any cease-fire further out and prolongs war-related risk premia.
insights.quote: Now that Ukrainian forces have stopped and partially reversed the Russian battlefield advance, the Kremlin appears to have embraced a new theory of victory.
insights.locator: Marking a new phase after almost
insights.speaker: Fredrik Wesslau

insights.claim: The decisive change in Russia's air campaign is not the number of weapons but the systematic widening of targets to railways, gas stations, ports, cargo ships, shopping malls, and data centers.
insights.so_what: Targeting economic logistics nodes threatens Ukraine's export capacity and fiscal base, not just front-line strength.
insights.quote: The big difference in Russia’s strategy, however, is not so much the types and numbers of missiles and drones. Rather, it is Russia’s systematic widening of the range of targets.
insights.locator: The big difference in Russia’s strategy
insights.speaker: Fredrik Wesslau

insights.claim: The author expects Russian strikes to rise further in frequency as additional weapons production comes online, with winter attacks likely intensifying on electricity, heating, and water infrastructure.
insights.so_what: A harsh winter campaign raises odds of Ukrainian economic distress and European spillover, including refugee flows.
insights.quote: In the weeks and months ahead, we should not only expect these strikes to continue but also rise further in frequency as additional Russian weapons production comes online.
insights.locator: In the weeks and months ahead
insights.speaker: Fredrik Wesslau

insights.claim: Without significantly more Western military and economic support, Putin will believe he has the upper hand, destroying the possibility of a cease-fire any time soon.
insights.so_what: Investors positioned for a Ukraine cease-fire or reconstruction trade face a longer timeline.
insights.quote: Otherwise, Putin will believe he has gained the upper hand, destroying the possibility of a cease-fire any time soon.
insights.locator: The Kremlin’s air war has put
insights.speaker: Fredrik Wesslau

insights.claim: Russia produces around 100 ballistic missiles per month, up from a handful in 2022 and expected to rise next year, while the US produces only about half that many Patriot interceptors per month.
insights.so_what: Structural interceptor scarcity is a durable tailwind for air-defense manufacturers and capacity expansion.
insights.quote: Russia currently produces around 100 ballistic missiles per month, up from just a handful per month in 2022 and expected to rise further by next year.
insights.speaker: Fredrik Wesslau

insights.claim: Patriot interceptor stocks are dwindling due to the war in the Middle East, making Washington reluctant to send more to Ukraine and Gulf states loath to give up theirs given the Iranian missile threat.
insights.so_what: Competing Middle East and Ukraine demand for interceptors tightens global air-defense supply.
insights.quote: With stocks dwindling due to the war in the Middle East, Washington has been reluctant to send any more interceptors to Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Fredrik Wesslau

insights.claim: There are not enough Patriot interceptors in the world to counter the volume of ballistic missiles Russia fires at Ukraine each month, so swap arrangements can only be a temporary stopgap.
insights.so_what: Points to sustained demand for new interceptor production lines and alternative missile-defense systems.
insights.quote: The fundamental problem is that there are not enough Patriot interceptors in the world to counter the number of ballistic missiles Russia is firing at Ukraine each month.
insights.speaker: Fredrik Wesslau

insights.claim: Russia's domestically produced jet-powered Shahed variant flies up to 375 mph, more than three times as fast as the original Iranian propeller drones, and uses mesh radio networks to evade Ukrainian electronic warfare.
insights.so_what: Faster, EW-resistant drones raise demand for new counter-drone interceptor technologies.
insights.quote: At speeds of up to 375 miles per hour, they can fly more than three times as fast as the original Iranian-supplied propeller drones, which makes them much harder to intercept.
insights.speaker: Fredrik Wesslau

insights.claim: The author proposes that Germany use its licensed Patriot PAC-2 production to arrange swaps in which the US or Gulf states ship interceptors to Ukraine now in exchange for later German output, and that Poland or Sweden be licensed to build PAC-3 interceptors for Ukraine if Trump refuses to license production to Kyiv.
insights.so_what: Licensed European PAC-3 production would expand the European defense-industrial base and order books.
insights.quote: a workaround could involve a trilateral agreement in which a third country—perhaps Poland or Sweden—is given a license to produce the more advanced PAC-3 interceptors
insights.locator: Trump has been reluctant to license
insights.speaker: Fredrik Wesslau

insights.claim: Ukraine and nine European states are developing a domestic anti-ballistic missile defense system under the Freyja initiative, but it could take years.
insights.so_what: A new European missile-defense program is a long-dated defense spending opportunity.
insights.quote: Together with nine European states, Kyiv is developing its own such systems as part of the Freyja initiative.
insights.speaker: Fredrik Wesslau

insights.claim: Given the global interceptor shortage, Ukraine's top priority should be degrading Russian missile production and launch infrastructure with Western intelligence and deep-strike capabilities, plus tighter sanctions on missile components.
insights.so_what: Implies more Western long-range strike supply and sanctions enforcement on component supply chains.
insights.quote: If you can’t intercept the arrow, hit the archer instead.
insights.speaker: Fredrik Wesslau

themes.theme: Damage to Ukraine's economy and trade

insights.claim: Russia has struck around 300 of Ukraine's 5,500 gas stations in six months, contributing to a roughly 50 percent rise in diesel prices since the start of the year, alongside the effect of Trump's war against Iran.
insights.so_what: Fuel-price inflation in Ukraine compounds economic damage and raises its import needs.
insights.quote: The price of diesel is up around 50 percent since the start of the year.
insights.speaker: Fredrik Wesslau

insights.claim: Russia has hit about 500 Ukrainian locomotives since 2022, more than half this year, undermining the railways that are Ukraine's lifeline with civilian airspace closed.
insights.so_what: Rail disruption impairs Ukrainian exports and domestic logistics.
insights.quote: Russia has also hit some 500 locomotives locomotives since 2022; more than half of these attacks took place this year.
insights.speaker: Fredrik Wesslau

insights.claim: Russia hit around 50 civilian cargo ships near Odesa over the summer, effectively shutting Ukraine's maritime egress so Ukrainian grain can no longer reach world markets via the Black Sea.
insights.so_what: Loss of the Black Sea grain corridor is a supply shock for global grain markets and a blow to Ukraine's export earnings.
insights.quote: Ukrainian grain is no longer able to reach the global market via the Black Sea, which is severely impacting Ukraine’s economy.
insights.locator: In the Black Sea port of Odesa
insights.speaker: Fredrik Wesslau

insights.claim: Ukrainian steel production fell nearly 60 percent year-over-year by August, and by late September three plants accounting for 90 percent of output had halted because of Russian strikes.
insights.so_what: Removal of Ukrainian steel from export markets tightens European steel supply.
insights.quote: By August, steel production was down nearly 60 percent year-over-year.
insights.speaker: Fredrik Wesslau

insights.claim: Economic collapse is draining Ukrainian tax revenues; Ukraine faces a projected 2026 budget deficit of $27 billion, partly fundable through the EU's Ukraine Plan tied to accession reforms.
insights.so_what: Ukraine's growing financing gap raises the fiscal burden on the EU budget.
insights.quote: Ukraine can plug some of its projected 2026 budget deficit of $27 billion with fresh money from the European Union
insights.speaker: Fredrik Wesslau

insights.claim: The EU's carbon tariffs imposed in January hit Ukraine's iron and steel exports, putting $4.7 billion of exports at risk between 2026 and 2030, so the author calls for a transitional waiver.
insights.so_what: Signals political pressure for CBAM carve-outs, a precedent relevant to EU carbon border policy.
insights.quote: putting the country at risk of losing $4.7 billion in exports between 2026 and 2030
insights.locator: Even as it funds Ukraine’s budget
insights.speaker: Fredrik Wesslau

insights.claim: The author argues the EU should treat a potential winter mass exodus of Ukrainian refugees as a deliberate Russian strategy to undermine European unity, and act pre-emptively by rebuilding energy infrastructure and storing Ukrainian gas.
insights.so_what: A refugee wave would stress European fiscal and political stability and could boost populist parties.
insights.quote: the EU should treat a potential mass exodus of refugees from Ukraine this winter as a deliberate Russian strategy to undermine European unity and political stability
insights.speaker: Fredrik Wesslau

insights.claim: Seventy percent of Ukraine's prewar electricity generation capacity has been destroyed.
insights.so_what: Indicates very large energy reconstruction needs and continued Ukrainian reliance on EU power imports.
insights.quote: with 70 percent of prewar generation capacity destroyed
insights.speaker: Fredrik Wesslau
